issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Mateo, a 22-year-old HVAC technician, first sought help after a year of increasing distress following a devastating accident at a commercial job site. He had been performing routine maintenance on a large rooftop unit when a heavy, poorly secured component he was working on unexpectedly detached, crashing down and severely injuring a co-worker below. The metallic shriek of the falling equipment, followed by the sickening thud and the sudden, chilling silence that descended afterwards, were seared into his mind. He remembered the coppery scent of blood mixing with the acrid smell of ozone from the damaged electrical wiring, smells that would later become potent triggers.

In the immediate aftermath, Mateo was overwhelmed by a crushing sense of guilt. He knew he could never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, a thought that gnawed at him relentlessly. His body, once a reliable instrument for his demanding trade, now felt like it had betrayed him, prone to sudden tremors and sweats, leading him to believe he could no longer trust his own physical reactions. When he looked in the mirror, he saw a stranger; the person he had become was unrecognisable to him, a hollowed-out version of his former self. These profound negative appraisals of himself and his actions quickly began to shape his behaviour. Because he felt he could never forgive himself and that his body was unreliable, Mateo started to avoid anything that could be stressful, fearing his reactions would lead to another disaster.

His avoidance became a rigid pattern. He found himself cancelling plans around specific dates or anniversaries connected to the event, often calling in sick to avoid the emotional burden. This constant avoidance of stressful situations, particularly at work, meant he often left tasks unfinished or delegated them, creating a general sense of unease and making him feel perpetually vulnerable to something dangerous happening. He also began overanalysing the details of the accident, going over and over what happened trying to make sense of it, replaying every second in his mind. Far from providing clarity, this obsessive overanalysing only solidified his belief that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him, trapping him further in his guilt and reinforcing his negative appraisals.

Despite his best efforts to suppress it, the memory of the accident would force its way into his mind when he least wanted it to, often triggered by the metallic clang of tools or the distinct smell of freon from a compressor, bringing back the olfactory recall of the pungent coolant and the coppery scent of blood from that day. These intrusive memories, especially when accompanied by the vivid smells, would immediately trigger strong physical reactions; his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he'd feel a surge of adrenaline, convincing him something dangerous was about to happen again. The constant state of hypervigilance and the physical reactivity he experienced kept the memory of the accident raw and vivid, making it feel alien, almost like it belonged to someone else, yet undeniably present and terrifyingly real. His deep-seated inaction guilt made the memory feel even more detached and alien, as if his mind was trying to distance itself from the unbearable reality of his perceived failure.

Mateo started to only feel safe in a very limited number of places – his small apartment, his mother’s house. Even a sudden, unusual silence at a job site, reminiscent of the silence after the crash, could make him feel that something dangerous was about to happen, sending a jolt of fear through him. His job, once a source of pride, became a minefield of triggers. He found himself unable to work in confined spaces, constantly on edge, his senses acutely tuned to any unexpected noise or smell, perpetually bracing for the next catastrophe.

The tightening grip of these cycles eventually brought Mateo to therapy. He was exhausted, isolated, and losing his ability to function at work. He feared he would never be able to trust himself again, that this unrecognisable self was permanent, and that he was destined to live a life haunted by the past, forever trapped by the memory of what he couldn't stop.
